cases.reason: The three capability URNs are contract text. A binding inventing its own spelling builds a request every JMAP server rejects.
MAX_BODY_VALUE_BYTES bounds what is asked of the server and PREVIEW_MAX_CHARS bounds what is returned to the caller. SS1.1 makes both a security property, not a tuning knob.
EMAIL_PROPERTIES is ORDERED and SS7 emits it verbatim, so the order is contract. A binding storing it in a set, or sorting it, builds a different request.

An array is NOT a record. This is what stops a JSON array being read as an object with numeric keys -- in JavaScript typeof [] is 'object', so the Array.isArray arm is load bearing; in Python isinstance(v, dict) gets it free.
typeof null is 'object' in JavaScript, so a null check is required and not implied.
THE rule SS3 predicts will be missed: absent and present-but-empty are the same condition. A binding whose as_string returns "" builds a session with apiUrl "" and then fetches it.
A JSON number is not a string. A binding coercing with str() or String() accepts it.
The happy path: apiUrl from the root, accountId from primaryAccounts[MAIL].
primaryAccounts must be a record; when it is not, the account id is an absence and so is the whole session.
A server offering core but not mail has no mail account to name.
There is no partially-populated session. A binding returning {apiUrl, accountId: None} hands the caller something it cannot use and will not notice until the POST.
Step 1: the value must be a record.

The return value is the PARSER'S serialisation, not the input string, so the value handed to a fetch is one this function actually inspected. Note the trailing slash the parser adds to a bare authority -- a binding returning the input fails here.
First of the three conditions, in evaluation order. The message is contract text (SSR5).
Second condition. Evaluated BEFORE the host check, so a non-https candidate on a mismatched host reports the scheme -- a binding checking host first reports the wrong one and fails this case.
Third condition, and the message interpolates BOTH hosts. A binding reporting only one, or reporting the full URLs, fails.

SSR6 says an absence; SS5.1 says this function is the exception and MUST raise. The distinction is the control: an absence is a value a caller can ignore, and the one thing a caller must not do with a rejected apiUrl is carry on. A binding returning None here passes every other §5 case -- they only compare messages -- and fails this one.

SS5.2 compares HOST only and requires https of the candidate alone, so an http base accepts an https candidate. Under an origin comparison -- scheme, host and port together, which url-resolution.md §6 uses -- this would be rejected. Pinned rather than corrected: the check is TIGHTER where it matters, since the candidate must be https regardless.

MEASURED cross-language hazard. JavaScript's URL.host DROPS a default port (:443 on https), while Python's .hostname + .port compose and Go's URL.Host both KEEP it. So this candidate is accepted by the reference and rejected by both naive ports -- a different verdict, not merely a different string. Caught by 0 of the other §5 cases, none of which carries an explicit port.

MEASURED cross-language hazard, and a DIFFERENT pair agrees than in the port case. JavaScript and Python lowercase the host; Go's URL.Host does NOT -- it returns API.Example.COM verbatim. So a naive Go rejects a candidate the other two accept.

MEASURED, and a third pairing again. JavaScript and Go keep the brackets around an IPv6 literal; Python's .hostname STRIPS them, so a naive compose yields 2001:db8::1:8443 -- not merely different but ambiguous, since nothing marks where the address ends.

The port is PART of the host for this comparison, so a genuine port difference rejects. The counterweight to the default-port case: a binding that dropped every port to make that one pass would accept this one.
One record exercising all nine members at once, so a binding dropping one fails here rather than only in whichever single-member case covers it.

THE asymmetry SS6 calls out: everywhere else an empty string becomes an absence, and here an absence becomes an empty string. A binding rejecting a record with no id -- the reasonable-looking choice -- fails this case.
The record is rejected ONLY when id and messageId are both absent. This is the boundary its sibling cases sit either side of.
The other side of the boundary: id alone is enough.
messageId is as-string of messageId[0] WHEN messageId is an array; a bare string is not an array and yields an absence. A binding accepting a string here reports a messageId the other two do not.
Both present: name, a space, and the email in angle brackets.
Name present, email empty: the result is the name alone, with no empty angle brackets.
Name absent: the result is the email.

THE dropping rule, stated by SS6.1 with this exact shape: three malformed entries yield an EMPTY list, not three empty strings. A binding mapping without filtering returns three. This is the opposite of SS6.2's rule for attachments, which is the next case's point.
A value that is not an array yields an empty list rather than raising.

The MIRROR of SS6.1's rule, and the reason both exist: attachments keep one entry per element INCLUDING non-records, so the returned length always equals the input length and a caller can rely on positional correspondence. A binding sharing one filtering helper between addresses and attachments fails one of these two whichever way it chooses.
The JMAP member is `type`; the view member is `mimeType`. A binding reading `mimeType` from the input finds nothing and reports an absence for every attachment.

Both infinities are ABSENT, not zero. A binding coercing with int(v or 0) reports 0 and loses the distinction between 'no size' and 'zero bytes'. Written as the literal 1e400, the convention the diagnostics corpus already set: JSON has no Infinity token, and a bare one is rejected by JSON.parse and by encoding/json even though Python accepts it as an extension. NaN cannot be written in JSON at all, so §6.2's NaN clause is unreachable from a case and stays with the bindings' own unit tests.
size must be a NUMBER. A JSON true is not a size -- and in Python bool is a subclass of int and math.isfinite(True) is True, so a binding checking finiteness before type reports sizeBytes 1 here.
A value that is not an array yields an empty list.
textBody is walked IN ORDER and the first part whose bodyValues entry has a non-empty value wins.
A part whose value is the empty string is not usable, so the walk continues. A binding stopping at the first part that EXISTS returns "" and never reaches the second.
With no usable body part the result is as-string of preview.
Step 1 requires bodyValues to be a RECORD and textBody to be an ARRAY; failing either goes straight to the fallback.
With nothing available the preview is the EMPTY STRING, never an absence -- the one member of the view that is a plain string rather than a nullable one.
Step 1 of five, in order.
Step 2: a run of spaces or tabs becomes ONE space. A binding collapsing all whitespace including newlines destroys the paragraph structure step 3 preserves.
Step 3: two or more newlines become one.
Step 4 trims per SSR7, which INCLUDES U+FEFF -- Python's str.strip() and Go's strings.TrimSpace do not remove it, so a delegating binding returns it in the preview.
Step 5: longer than PREVIEW_MAX_CHARS is truncated to it.

THE case this corpus exists for. SS6.4 forbids truncation splitting a code point, and the reference slices at UTF-16 code unit 2000 -- which here is the LOW half of a surrogate pair, leaving a lone high surrogate and an ill-formed string that cannot be encoded as UTF-8 at all. The three languages fail differently on the same expression: TypeScript strands a surrogate, Go's byte slice cuts a 4-byte lead, and Python is correct by construction because its unit IS the code point. Expected output keeps 1999 units and drops the straddling character whole. Caught by 0 of the 69 existing jmap unit tests.

The list form omits filter ENTIRELY -- not null, not {}. A binding emitting filter: null sends a request the server may reject or interpret differently, and the difference is invisible in a structural comparison unless a case pins the absence.
The search form differs from list in exactly one member.

"q" appears twice -- the query's client id and the get's resultOf -- and they MUST agree. A mismatch produces an unresolved-reference error from the server at runtime against a live account, which is the worst place to find it. Pinned structurally so a rename in one copy fails here instead.
TWO method calls in ONE request. A binding issuing the get separately doubles the round trips and loses the back-reference entirely.
The get form: ids as a one-element array, client id "e", and no query call.
The shared Email/get arguments, including bodyProperties in order. maxBodyValueBytes is what bounds the body the server sends, so SS1.1 makes it a security property.
methodResponses is scanned IN ORDER for the first element whose first item equals the name. A binding scanning backwards, or building a dict keyed by name, returns the last.
No match yields an absence rather than raising.
A JMAP error response carries the method name `error`, so it simply does not match -- the tolerant path SSR6 requires, with no special-casing.
A matching name whose second item is not a record yields an absence.
extractEmailList returns an EMPTY LIST, not an absence, when list is not an array -- the one place in SS8 where the two differ.
The ordinary case, so the empty-list case above is not the only coverage.
methodResponses must be an array; when it is not, an absence.
